1002.title: Hebrew spoken again
1002.hook: Eliezer Ben-Yehuda helps revive Hebrew as a daily language
1002.howItsDone: Hebrew is the language of Jewish prayer and Torah study around the world, and in Israel it is also the everyday spoken language; Jews outside Israel may learn some Hebrew for prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the whole argument, and your line: a table full of argument. Did you hear out someone you disagree with? Today, something the movement built that outlasted many of its arguments: a spoken language. Day one thousand two.

Ask for an ice cream in Tel Aviv, a bus ticket in Haifa, a phone charger in Jerusalem, and you'll do it in Hebrew. It sounds ordinary. But for a long stretch of history, few people asked for bread in Hebrew. They prayed in it. They studied Torah and Talmud in it. Scholars wrote letters and poems in it across oceans. But at the kitchen table, Jews spoke Yiddish, Ladino, Arabic, Persian, German, Russian. Hebrew was for heaven and for books. Then a stubborn man in Jerusalem decided his kitchen would be different. Today, Hebrew spoken again.
screen: `ICE CREAM IN HEBREW.` → `A LANGUAGE FOR PRAYER AND BOOKS.` → `A STUBBORN KITCHEN IN JERUSALEM.`

segments.voice: His name was Eliezer Ben-Yehuda. He grew up in the Russian Empire, studied in Paris, and came to Jerusalem with one fixed idea: a people returning to its land should speak its own language there, every day, about everything. So he did it at home. As the family story goes, he and his wife raised their son speaking only Hebrew, and he would not let other languages be spoken around the boy. Visitors found it strange. Some religious neighbors were upset, because to them Hebrew was a holy tongue, not something for shopping lists. But a daily language needs daily words, and the old books had no words for many of the things in a modern street or house. So Ben-Yehuda published his own Hebrew newspapers, and he spent his life on an enormous dictionary, collecting words from the Bible, the Mishnah and later writings, and proposing new ones where nothing old would do. Here is the part the legend sometimes leaves out. He did not do it alone. Teachers in the new farming villages taught their classes in Hebrew. Children carried it home to parents who had come from everywhere. Families, schools and writers made it stick. The prophet Zephaniah has a line about a day when God will turn to the peoples a pure language, so that all may call on God's name. Ben-Yehuda's dream was more modest and more strange: a language of prayer, at last, used to ask someone to pass the salt.
screen: `ONE STUBBORN KITCHEN.` · `NEW WORDS FROM OLD BOOKS.` · `TEACHERS AND CHILDREN MADE IT STICK.` · then, large: `PASS THE SALT, IN HEBREW.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: say one Hebrew word today. Let's choose it now. Settle, and breathe. Try shalom, which means peace, and is also hello and goodbye. Or todah, which means thank you. Say it once, quietly, out loud. Notice the shape of it in your mouth. Then sit with it. This word was in prayer books long before it was in shops. Now it is in both. When the bell rings, decide who will hear it from you today. The bell holds the time.
Ben-Yehuda. The man who insisted his family, and then a people, speak Hebrew every day, from the kitchen table to the street, and spent his life writing a dictionary for it. Today's word.
Your line: pass the salt, in Hebrew. Today, say your Hebrew word to one person, or write it on a note where you'll see it. Day one thousand two.

1003.title: The kibbutz
1003.hook: collective farms built on shared work
1003.howItsDone: Kibbutz members have traditionally shared work, meals and decisions through a general meeting; some kibbutzim are religious and keep Shabbat together, and some have changed their economic arrangements over time.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a language of prayer at the kitchen table, and your line: pass the salt, in Hebrew. Who heard your Hebrew word? Today, a Hebrew word that became a whole way of living. Day one thousand three.

A long dining hall at dusk. Rows of tables, the same plates, the same bread, a hum of people who have worked the same fields since sunrise. Nobody pays at the door. Nobody gets a bill. The person who drove the tractor today might be serving soup tomorrow, and the person serving soup today might be on the tractor. On the wall, a notice for the evening meeting, where everyone gets a vote. This is a kibbutz, and for the young people who built the early ones, this room was the point.
screen: `A LONG DINING HALL.` → `NOBODY GETS A BILL.` → `A MEETING WHERE EVERYONE VOTES.`

segments.voice: Kibbutz is a Hebrew word for a gathering, a group. It shares its root with the word the Torah uses when it promises that God will gather the scattered people back from among the nations. The kibbutz took that old verb and made it a farm. The idea was simple and radical. The members held their property and their earnings in common, not as separate families. They ate together. They shared the work, and jobs often rotated, so nobody was only ever the boss or only ever the dishwasher. Big decisions went to the general meeting, where every member had a voice. Money, clothes, sometimes even the raising of children were arranged in common. The founders of the early ones came out of the labor Zionism of two lessons ago: young people who believed that working the soil with their own hands would heal something in them and in their people. There were also religious kibbutzim, where members shared the work and also kept Shabbat and prayed together. Life was hard: swamps, heat, sickness, arguments. And the kibbutz has changed over the years; some now pay members different salaries and run factories as well as farms. Older members sometimes argue about whether the change was wise. But the picture stays. The psalm puts it in one line, and a song built on it is still sung at Jewish gatherings: "Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!" The psalm calls it good and pleasant. The kibbutz found out it was also work.
screen: `A GATHERING, A GROUP.` · `SHARED WORK, SHARED TABLE.` · `EVERY MEMBER A VOTE.` · `A KIBBUTZ THAT CHANGED.` · then, large: `GOOD AND PLEASANT, AND ALSO WORK.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: share one thing. Settle, and breathe. Run through your day in your mind and find one thing you usually keep for yourself: a meal, a car ride, a skill, an hour, a good book. Nothing grand. Then picture one person who could use it, or simply enjoy it with you. See yourself offering it. Notice whether it feels like losing something or gaining something, or both. Choose the person, and choose the thing. The bell holds the time.
Kibbutz. A gathering, a group: a community that shared its work, its table and its decisions, sometimes secular, sometimes religious. Today's word.
Your line: together. Today, share the one thing you chose, and if you can, share a meal at the same table. Day one thousand three.

1004.title: Rav Kook
1004.hook: a mystic chief rabbi who saw holiness in secular pioneers
1004.howItsDone: Rav Kook's writings are studied in religious Zionist yeshivas and beyond, and his teaching that holiness can be found in secular life is quoted well beyond those circles, while others disagree with it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the kibbutz, and your line: together. Did you share the thing you chose? Today, a rabbi who looked at those secular farmers and saw something they might not have seen in themselves. Day one thousand four.

On a Friday evening, a group of young pioneers finish work late in the fields. No candles, no kiddush, no synagogue. Some of them left religion behind on purpose. Down the road lives a rabbi who keeps the commandments with great care and writes mystical poetry. A rabbi like that might be expected to scold them. Instead he speaks of them with something close to love. He says their sweat in the soil is holy work, even if they would never use that word. His name is Rabbi Abraham Isaac Kook. He is known as Rav Kook.
screen: `PIONEERS WITHOUT CANDLES.` → `A RABBI WHO WRITES MYSTICAL POETRY.` → `HOLY WORK, WITHOUT THE WORD.`

segments.voice: Rav Kook came to the land of Israel as the rabbi of the port city of Jaffa, and later became chief rabbi under British rule. He was a legal scholar, but also a mystic, and his mysticism drew on an old Kabbalah teaching. In that teaching, when the world was made, sparks of divine light scattered and fell into everything, even into places that look empty of God. The work of a person is to find those sparks and lift them up. Rav Kook looked at the young secular pioneers, the labor Zionists, the kibbutz builders, and said: there are sparks in this too. Their longing for justice, their love of the land, their willingness to give up comfort for their people. To him these were holy, even when the people carrying them denied any holiness at all. A saying often linked to him sums up his hope: the old will be made new, and the new will be made holy. Not everyone was happy with this. Some rabbis thought he was far too generous to people who broke the Sabbath. Some pioneers did not want to be told that their work was secretly religious. Rav Kook kept to his view. There is a line in Genesis that fits him. Jacob wakes from his dream of the ladder and says, "Surely the LORD is in this place; and I knew it not." Rav Kook looked at people who did not know, and believed it anyway.
screen: `A RABBI AND A MYSTIC.` · `SPARKS SCATTERED IN EVERYTHING.` · `HOLINESS IN THE PIONEERS.` · `NOT EVERYONE AGREED.` · then, large: `AND I KNEW IT NOT.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: see holiness in someone unlikely. Settle, and let your breath slow. Think of someone you don't naturally admire, maybe someone whose choices you don't share, or who would laugh at the word holy. Now look for one spark in them: a loyalty, a kindness, a stubborn honesty, a love they carry. You don't have to approve of everything. Just find the spark and hold it in view, the way Rav Kook held the pioneers. The bell holds the time.
Rav Kook. Rabbi Abraham Isaac Kook, a mystic and chief rabbi who saw sparks of holiness in secular pioneers. Today's word.
Your line: sparks in the secular. Today, tell the person you thought of, or someone like them, one good thing you see in them. Day one thousand four.

1005.title: Before we begin
1005.hook: the next sessions tell of the Holocaust, the Shoah; go slowly and stop whenever you need
1005.howItsDone: Jewish communities remember the Shoah on Yom HaShoah, Holocaust Remembrance Day, with candles, the reading of names, survivors' testimony and memorial prayers; in Israel a siren sounds and people stand in silence.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rav Kook, and your line: sparks in the secular. Did you tell someone one good thing you see in them? Today is different. Today is a doorway, and we stand in it for a moment before going through. Day one thousand five.

Before a hard conversation, people often pause at the door. They take a breath. They put down whatever they were carrying. That's what today is. The next sessions on this path tell of the Holocaust, the murder of Europe's Jews by Nazi Germany and those who helped it. Some listeners carry this history in their own families. Some are meeting it closely for the first time. Either way, it is heavy. So today there is no history lesson. Just a word, a way of walking, and permission to stop.
screen: `A PAUSE AT THE DOOR.` → `THE NEXT SESSIONS.` → `PERMISSION TO STOP.`

segments.voice: Shoah is a Hebrew word. It is the name Jews in Israel, and Jews elsewhere too, use for the Holocaust. It is not a new word. It appears in the Bible, where the prophet Zephaniah describes a day of ruin and desolation, a day of darkness. A biblical word for devastation, carried forward to name what happened. Some people use the English word Holocaust. Some prefer Shoah, a word from their own language and their own Scripture. Both are used, with respect. Now, the way of walking. The Bible has a picture of how to come near great suffering. When Job has lost almost everything, three friends come to comfort him. And the first thing they do is not speak. The text says they sat with him on the ground for seven days and seven nights, and no one said a word, because they saw how great his pain was. Silence first. Words later. That is how these sessions will try to go. They will tell real history, honestly, and with care. They will begin with how people lived, not only how they died. They will say names when names are known. They will not use horror to hold your attention. And here is the most important part. You may stop whenever you need. You may skip a day and come back. You may listen with someone beside you. Going slowly is not failing. In this history, going gently is a way of honoring the people in it.
screen: `SHOAH: A BIBLICAL WORD FOR RUIN.` · `JOB'S FRIENDS SAT IN SILENCE.` · `LIVES, NAMES, CARE.` · then, large: `YOU MAY STOP WHENEVER YOU NEED.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: decide how you'll care for yourself. Sit comfortably and let your breath settle. Ask yourself a few plain questions, and let the answers come slowly. What time of day is best for listening to something heavy? Who could you talk to if a session stays with you? What helps you come back to yourself: a walk, a cup of tea, a call, a prayer, if you pray? Choose one thing you'll do after each of the next sessions. The bell holds the time.
Shoah. The Hebrew name for the Holocaust, a biblical word for ruin and devastation, used with care. Today's word.
Your line: go gently. Today, tell one person you trust that you'll be learning about this, so you're not carrying it alone. Day one thousand five.

1006.title: They lived
1006.hook: Jews lived full lives in Europe's cities and towns
1006.howItsDone: Museums, archives and Jewish communities collect photographs, letters and memorial books from prewar Jewish towns and cities, so that remembrance includes how people lived, not only how they died.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a doorway, a word, Shoah, and your line: go gently. Did you choose how you'll care for yourself? Keep it close. Today begins where yesterday promised, with life. Day one thousand six.

A black-and-white photo. A boy on a bicycle on a cobbled street, grinning, his cap pushed back. Behind him a shop sign in Hebrew letters, a woman leaning out of a window, two men arguing on a corner with their hands. Nobody in the picture is posing for history. They're just having a Tuesday. It's easy to meet the Jews of prewar Europe only through how their world ended. This session meets them first as they were: alive, busy, and not waiting for anything. Today, they lived.
screen: `A BOY ON A BICYCLE.` → `JUST HAVING A TUESDAY.` → `MEET THEM AS THEY WERE.`

segments.voice: Jewish Europe was not one place. It was big cities: Warsaw, Vilna, Budapest, Berlin, Amsterdam, Salonika, Paris. And it was small market towns across Eastern Europe, the kind Yiddish calls a shtetl, a little town, where Jews and their neighbors traded on market day. It was not one kind of Jew either. There were Hasidim gathered around their rebbes, singing at long tables. There were yeshiva students arguing over the Talmud late into the night. There were Jewish socialists organizing unions, and Zionists, from the last few lessons, learning Hebrew and dreaming of the land. There were Jews who kept little of the tradition and thought of themselves as Germans or French. There were Yiddish newspapers and theaters, poets and comedians, soccer clubs and summer camps, doctors, tailors, scholars, grocers, and children doing homework at kitchen tables. They fell in love. They fought about politics. They worried about rent. They celebrated weddings and argued with their grandparents. Photographers walked those streets, and some of their pictures survive, faces looking back at us across the years. The Torah has a line, spoken by Moses to the people at the edge of the land, setting life and death before them: "therefore choose life." This lesson is a small choice like that. Before the next sessions tell what was done to these communities, they deserve to be met alive. Not as victims first. As neighbors. As people with Tuesday plans. They lived.
screen: `CITIES AND SMALL TOWNS.` · `MANY KINDS OF JEWS.` · `LOVE, POLITICS, RENT, WEDDINGS.` · then, large: `THEREFORE CHOOSE LIFE.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: look at one old photo of a community. If you have one, a family picture or one you can find later, hold it now. If you don't, use the boy on the bicycle. Sit with it, and breathe. Choose one face. Wonder about one ordinary thing: what they ate that day, what made them laugh, who they were going home to. Give them a whole life in your mind, not just an ending. The bell holds the time.
They lived. The Jews of prewar Europe, in cities and small towns, of every kind, met first as people living full lives. Today's word.
Your line: just having a Tuesday. Today, find one photo of a Jewish community from before the war, and look at it for one full minute. Day one thousand six.

1007.hook: the Nazis take power, and German Jews begin to lose jobs and rights, one rule at a time
1007.howItsDone: Jewish communities, schools and Holocaust museums teach the years before the war as part of the story, some by reading the laws and decrees of the time alongside the stories of families who lived under them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, your line was just having a Tuesday: whole communities, with their bakeries and arguments and weddings. Did you find a face in an old photo? Hold onto it today, gently. Go slowly, and stop whenever you need. Day one thousand seven.

Before any fire, there was paper. A teacher in a German city opens an official letter: his post is ended. Across town, a shopkeeper unlocks his door in the morning and finds a man in uniform standing outside it, next to a painted sign telling customers not to buy from Jews. A lawyer is told he can no longer appear in court. Nothing has been burned yet. It is signs, letters, forms, stamps. Paper. Today's title is a year, and this is what it looked like from the inside: 1933.
screen: `A LETTER ENDING A JOB.` → `A SIGN OUTSIDE THE SHOP.` → `PAPER, NOT FIRE. NOT YET.`

segments.voice: In 1933 the Nazi party came to power in Germany. What came first was not violence on every street. It was rules. That spring there was a national boycott of Jewish shops, doctors and lawyers, with uniformed men posted at the doors. Then a law pushed Jewish officials out of government service: judges, teachers, clerks. Rules limited how many Jewish students schools would take. Books by Jewish writers, and by others the regime disliked, were thrown onto bonfires in public squares. Step by step, much of it was printed, signed and stamped, and each step was a little smaller than the shock it should have caused. That is part of what makes this year hard to read. People woke up each morning in the same house, on the same street, with one thing fewer. The Torah has a line that runs straight against all of it. "Ye shall have one manner of law, as well for the stranger, as for the home-born." One law. The same rights for the person who belongs and the person who arrives. What began in Germany in 1933 was the opposite: one law for some citizens and another for their Jewish neighbors, who had been citizens too. Families had to decide what this meant, with no way of seeing ahead. Some left. Some stayed, hoping it would pass. Reading it now, we know what came next. They didn't. That is why today's line is quiet and plain: rights can be taken. Not only by armies, but by paper, one rule at a time, while ordinary life goes on around it.
screen: `FIRST CAME RULES.` · `A BOYCOTT, A DISMISSAL, A BONFIRE.` · `ONE LAW FOR ALL, SAYS THE TORAH.` · `NO WAY TO SEE AHEAD.` · then, large: `ONE MANNER OF LAW.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: notice one right you have. Sit comfortably and let your breath slow. Bring to mind one right you rarely think about. To go to school. To keep your job. To walk into any shop. To pray in your own way, or not at all. To vote. Choose one, and hold it for a while. Notice who and what keeps it in place for you: a law, a court, the neighbors who would object if it were taken. If your mind turns to the families of 1933, let it, and then come back to your breath. Rest here until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Boycott. The national campaign in 1933 against Jewish shops, doctors and lawyers that opened the door to law after law stripping Jews of their rights. Today's word.
Your line: rights can be taken. Today, when you use a right without thinking, a vote, a seat in a class, an open door, notice it once. Day one thousand seven.

1008.title: Kristallnacht (1938)
1008.hook: in one night, synagogues burn, shop windows are smashed, and Jewish men are arrested
1008.howItsDone: Jewish communities remember Kristallnacht each year with candles, readings and memorial services, often in synagogues, and some light memorial candles in their windows.

segments.voice: Yesterday, boycott, and your line: rights can be taken. Did you notice a right of yours in use, a vote, a seat, an open door? Today the paper turns to fire. Go gently. Day one thousand eight.

Morning, after a long night. A street in a German town is covered in glass. It crunches under shoes. The windows of the Jewish-owned shops are gone, and the goods inside are thrown across the pavement. At the end of the street, where the synagogue stood, there is smoke. Fire engines are parked nearby, and the firefighters are hosing down the house next door. Not the synagogue. They have been told to let it burn. In homes across the town, Jewish men are missing, taken in the night. Today's word is the name that night was given.
screen: `A STREET COVERED IN GLASS.` → `THE SYNAGOGUE ON FIRE.` → `THE MEN TAKEN AWAY.`

segments.voice: Kristallnacht. It's German for crystal night, and people often call it the night of broken glass, for what lay on the streets the next morning. In 1938, across Germany and Austria, mobs and men in uniform set synagogues on fire, smashed the windows of Jewish shops, broke into Jewish homes and beat the people inside. Torah scrolls, written by hand and carried for generations, were thrown into the flames. Jewish men were arrested and sent to concentration camps. Then came the part that is hard to believe. The regime declared that the Jews themselves were to blame, and made the Jewish community pay for the damage. Some people today prefer another name for that night, the November pogrom, because crystal sounds almost pretty, and the word can hide what happened. Both names are used. In Hebrew it is often called leil ha-bedolach, the night of crystal. That night the persecution came openly, in the street, in fire, while neighbors watched. For Jewish families still in Germany, the question pressed harder than ever: not whether to leave, but how. The book of Proverbs has a line about a different kind of fire. "The spirit of man is the lamp of the LORD." A lamp is a small fire that gives light instead of destroying. Some remember this night with candles: in synagogues, at memorials, in windows. A small flame, lit on purpose, answering the large one.
screen: `CRYSTAL NIGHT: THE GLASS ON THE STREETS.` · `SYNAGOGUES BURNED, MEN ARRESTED.` · `TWO NAMES FOR ONE NIGHT.` · `A SMALL FLAME ANSWERS A LARGE ONE.` · then, large: `THE SPIRIT OF MAN IS THE LAMP OF THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: light a candle. If you have one, and it's safe where you are, light it now and set it in front of you. If you don't, look at any small light: a lamp, a screen turned low, the sky through a window. Sit and let your breath slow. Watch the flame move. Let it stand for the synagogues that burned, and for the people who prayed in them. If you pray, you can say the line from Proverbs quietly: the spirit of man is the lamp of the LORD. If you don't, just watch the light until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Kristallnacht. Crystal night, the night of broken glass: synagogues burned, Jewish shops and homes smashed, Jewish men arrested, across Germany and Austria in 1938. Today's word.

Your line: the night of glass. Today, if you pass a lit window or a candle, let it remind you of the small flames lit to remember. This week ran from Ben-Yehuda and the kibbutz to the edge of the Shoah: just having a Tuesday, boycott, and now the glass. Rest whenever you need to. Day one thousand eight.

what it means: crystal night, the night synagogues burned and Jewish shops and homes were smashed across Germany and Austria in 1938.
what a scholar hears: two names for one night, and why some prefer the November pogrom: crystal can sound pretty and hide what happened.
